\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary synthetic text detection, providing a framework for characterizing the provenance of web-crawled text at finer granularity.
Across six generators from three model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), we documented differential depth response: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble combining both feature types achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination across six base-model generators, with per-generator std of 0.051.
We also reported that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling, establishing that, in our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting functions as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization rather than a curative tool for data selection.

Future work should extend evaluation to instruction-tuned and RLHF models, frontier-scale generators (70B+), and multilingual settings.
All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication to facilitate reproducibility.

1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
5	
6	\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
7	\label{sec:results-classification}
8	
9	Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.
10	
11	The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.789 (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), the gen-0 class F1 (0.94) may be inflated; we therefore report a leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, F1\,=\,0.723) as the primary metric in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}.
12	Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
13	Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.
14	
15	\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
16	The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
17	However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
18	Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
19	Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+0.8\,pp to 0.810), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
20	A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
21	We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
24	Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).
25	
26	\paragraph{Cross-model chains.}
27	Real-world contamination involves diverse generators at each depth step.
28	We construct cross-model chains where each generation step uses a randomly selected generator and evaluate under LOGO cross-validation.
29	Cross-model chains yield 3-class macro-F1\,=\,0.809 and binary F1\,=\,0.764, confirming that depth signal is maintained when chain provenance is heterogeneous.
30	Cross-model 3-class F1 (0.809) falls below the best single-model ceiling (Pythia-1B, 0.862) but demonstrates that depth fingerprinting remains effective in multi-generator scenarios that better approximate real-world web contamination.
31	
32	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
33	Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
34	Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

59	\paragraph{Ordinal regression comparison.}
60	To test whether the ordinal structure of the 3-class depth label provides additional discriminative power, we compare CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral_ordinal} and Frank-Hall ordinal reduction \cite{frank_hall_ordinal} against the standard multiclass XGBoost classifier under the same LOGO protocol.

67	\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
68	\label{sec:results-differential}
69	
70	Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
71	This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).
72	
73	\begin{figure}[t]
74	\centering
75	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
76	\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Central-tendency and diversity features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show strong monotonic drift, while shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain near-stationary.}
77	\label{fig:feature-drift}
78	\end{figure}

80	Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
81	drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),
82	while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.089$).
83	
84	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
85	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
86	The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
87	Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.269), followed by entropy mean (0.164) and TTR (0.159).
88	Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.
89	
90	\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
91	To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
92	All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
93	The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.

97	\centering
98	\small
99	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
100	\toprule
101	\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
102	\midrule
103	Full (7 features)     & 0.789 & hapax\_ratio (0.269) \\
104	Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
105	Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
106	\bottomrule
107	\end{tabular}

109	\label{tab:ablation}
110	\end{table}

115	\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
116	\label{sec:results-baselines}
117	
118	\begin{figure}[t]
119	\centering
120	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.png}
121	\caption{LOGO macro-F1 with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals for each detection baseline and the 7-feature ensemble. Per-generator held-out F1 varies more for single detectors than for the ensemble.}
122	\label{fig:baseline-ci}
123	\end{figure}
124	
125	We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation.
126	Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), 3-class LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
127	We therefore report both 3-class and binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) results; the binary metric is the primary measure of depth discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).
128	
129	\begin{table}[t]
130	\centering
131	\small
132	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
133	\toprule
134	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{Per-gen std} \\
135	\midrule
136	7-feature ensemble    & 0.789 & \textbf{0.723} & 0.051 \\
137	4-det.\ + surface     & \textbf{0.805} & 0.724 & 0.049 \\
138	4-detector ens.\      & 0.796 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
139	Avg-LogProb           & 0.737 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
140	LD-Score              & 0.655 & 0.701 & 0.045 \\
141	FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & 0.616 & 0.056 \\
142	Binoculars            & 0.417 & 0.524 & 0.022 \\
143	\bottomrule
144	\end{tabular}
145	\caption{Depth classification under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. \textbf{3-class}: gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ (gen-0 samples shared across generators; see \S\ref{sec:generation}). \textbf{Binary}: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ only, eliminating the gen-0 train--test overlap. Per-gen std measures cross-generator consistency of the binary metric. The 7-feature ensemble is the strongest single-model method on both metrics and matches the best multi-detector ensemble on binary F1.}
146	\label{tab:baselines}
147	\end{table}
148	
149	The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723, outperforming every individual detection baseline: +1.1\,pp over Avg-LogProb, +2.2\,pp over LD-Score, +10.7\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +19.9\,pp over Binoculars ($p < 0.001$ for all comparisons).
150	On the 3-class metric, the ensemble (0.789) similarly outperforms all single baselines, though the margins are inflated by the gen-0 overlap.
151	
152	\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
153	Combining all four detection scores into a 4-detector ensemble yields binary F1\,=\,0.712---below the 7-feature ensemble (0.723).
154	The multi-detector advantage seen in 3-class evaluation (0.796 vs.\ 0.789) is driven entirely by superior gen-0 classification; existing detectors excel at human-vs-machine discrimination but do not capture the finer depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+.
155	Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble raises binary F1 to 0.724, matching the 7-feature ensemble and confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
156	Baseline results are stable across classifier hyperparameters: using the ensemble's settings ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$) instead of the default ($100$/$3$) changes baseline F1 by less than 0.002\,pp, confirming that performance differences reflect feature informativeness rather than classifier capacity.
157	
158	\paragraph{Binoculars: a non-transferable signal.}
159	Binoculars achieves near-random performance on the depth task (3-class F1\,=\,0.417, binary F1\,=\,0.524), confirming that cross-model perplexity ratios---the core signal in Binoculars---do not transfer to depth discrimination.
160	
161	
162	\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
163	\label{sec:results-downstream}
164	
165	Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
166	We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).
167	
168	\begin{table}[t]
169	\centering
170	\small
171	\begin{tabular}{lrc}
172	\toprule
173	\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
174	\midrule
175	All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
176	Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
177	Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
178	Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
179	Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
180	\bottomrule
181	\end{tabular}
182	\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
183	\label{tab:downstream}
184	\end{table}
185	
186	The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
187	Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
188	At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
189	Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.
190	
191	Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.
192	
193	We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
194	Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}

However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.

Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+0.8\,pp to 0.810), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.

Cross-model 3-class F1 (0.809) falls below the best single-model ceiling (Pythia-1B, 0.862) but demonstrates that depth fingerprinting remains effective in multi-generator scenarios that better approximate real-world web contamination.

We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation.
Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), 3-class LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
We therefore report both 3-class and binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) results; the binary metric is the primary measure of depth discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{Per-gen std} \\
\midrule
7-feature ensemble    & 0.789 & \textbf{0.723} & 0.051 \\
4-det.\ + surface     & \textbf{0.805} & 0.724 & 0.049 \\
4-detector ens.\      & 0.796 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
Avg-LogProb           & 0.737 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
LD-Score              & 0.655 & 0.701 & 0.045 \\
FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & 0.616 & 0.056 \\
Binoculars            & 0.417 & 0.524 & 0.022 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Depth classification under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. \textbf{3-class}: gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ (gen-0 samples shared across generators; see \S\ref{sec:generation}). \textbf{Binary}: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ only, eliminating the gen-0 train--test overlap. Per-gen std measures cross-generator consistency of the binary metric. The 7-feature ensemble is the strongest single-model method on both metrics and matches the best multi-detector ensemble on binary F1.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723, outperforming every individual detection baseline: +1.1\,pp over Avg-LogProb, +2.2\,pp over LD-Score, +10.7\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +19.9\,pp over Binoculars ($p < 0.001$ for all comparisons).
On the 3-class metric, the ensemble (0.789) similarly outperforms all single baselines, though the margins are inflated by the gen-0 overlap.

\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
Combining all four detection scores into a 4-detector ensemble yields binary F1\,=\,0.712---below the 7-feature ensemble (0.723).
The multi-detector advantage seen in 3-class evaluation (0.796 vs.\ 0.789) is driven entirely by superior gen-0 classification; existing detectors excel at human-vs-machine discrimination but do not capture the finer depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+.
Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble raises binary F1 to 0.724, matching the 7-feature ensemble and confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
Baseline results are stable across classifier hyperparameters: using the ensemble's settings ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$) instead of the default ($100$/$3$) changes baseline F1 by less than 0.002\,pp, confirming that performance differences reflect feature informativeness rather than classifier capacity.

\paragraph{Binoculars: a non-transferable signal.}
Binoculars achieves near-random performance on the depth task (3-class F1\,=\,0.417, binary F1\,=\,0.524), confirming that cross-model perplexity ratios---the core signal in Binoculars---do not transfer to depth discrimination.


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary synthetic text detection, providing a framework for characterizing the provenance of web-crawled text at finer granularity.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.789 (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), the gen-0 class F1 (0.94) may be inflated; we therefore report a leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, F1\,=\,0.723) as the primary metric in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}.
Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.

\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+0.8\,pp to 0.810), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.

\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).

\paragraph{Cross-model chains.}
Real-world contamination involves diverse generators at each depth step.
We construct cross-model chains where each generation step uses a randomly selected generator and evaluate under LOGO cross-validation.
Cross-model chains yield 3-class macro-F1\,=\,0.809 and binary F1\,=\,0.764, confirming that depth signal is maintained when chain provenance is heterogeneous.
Cross-model 3-class F1 (0.809) falls below the best single-model ceiling (Pythia-1B, 0.862) but demonstrates that depth fingerprinting remains effective in multi-generator scenarios that better approximate real-world web contamination.

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Held-out F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia & 1.0B & 0.856 & [0.843, 0.863] \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia & 2.8B & 0.804 & [0.793, 0.813] \\
OLMo-2-1B      & OLMo   & 1.5B & 0.764 & [0.754, 0.776] \\
Qwen3-0.6B     & Qwen   & 0.6B & 0.824 & [0.813, 0.834] \\
Qwen3-1.7B     & Qwen   & 1.7B & 0.806 & [0.796, 0.817] \\
Qwen3-8B       & Qwen   & 8.2B & 0.683 & [0.668, 0.694] \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (6-gen LOGO)} & 0.789 & --- \\
\multicolumn{3}{l}{5-gen LOGO (excl.\ Qwen3-8B)} & 0.802 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals ($n$\,=\,1000) for 3-class depth estimation using the 7-feature ensemble. Each row holds out one generator for testing and trains on the remaining five.}
\label{tab:logo-results}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Ordinal regression comparison.}
To test whether the ordinal structure of the 3-class depth label provides additional discriminative power, we compare CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral_ordinal} and Frank-Hall ordinal reduction \cite{frank_hall_ordinal} against the standard multiclass XGBoost classifier under the same LOGO protocol.
On 3-class F1, CORAL achieves 0.771, Frank-Hall 0.793, and XGBoost 0.789; all three confidence intervals overlap.
Binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) similarly shows no separation: XGBoost 0.721, CORAL 0.728.
Concordance index---an ordinal-specific metric rewarding correct ranking---yields XGBoost 0.821, CORAL 0.810, Frank-Hall 0.825; again, all CIs overlap.
The standard multiclass classifier already captures the depth-discriminative signal, and explicitly encoding ordinal structure does not yield a measurable gain, likely because the 3-class granularity provides insufficient ordinal resolution for ranking-aware losses to exploit.


\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Central-tendency and diversity features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show strong monotonic drift, while shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain near-stationary.}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),
while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.089$).

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.269), followed by entropy mean (0.164) and TTR (0.159).
Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
\midrule
Full (7 features)     & 0.789 & hapax\_ratio (0.269) \\
Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Feature ablation (6-gen LOGO). Full $>$ surface = reference confirms complementarity between surface diversity features and reference-model distributional features.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Leave-one-feature-out analysis confirms that 6 of 7 features contribute positively, with entropy\_max showing the largest marginal impact despite modest split frequency (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.png}
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals for each detection baseline and the 7-feature ensemble. Per-generator held-out F1 varies more for single detectors than for the ensemble.}
\label{fig:baseline-ci}
\end{figure}

We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation.
Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), 3-class LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
We therefore report both 3-class and binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) results; the binary metric is the primary measure of depth discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{Per-gen std} \\
\midrule
7-feature ensemble    & 0.789 & \textbf{0.723} & 0.051 \\
4-det.\ + surface     & \textbf{0.805} & 0.724 & 0.049 \\
4-detector ens.\      & 0.796 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
Avg-LogProb           & 0.737 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
LD-Score              & 0.655 & 0.701 & 0.045 \\
FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & 0.616 & 0.056 \\
Binoculars            & 0.417 & 0.524 & 0.022 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Depth classification under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. \textbf{3-class}: gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ (gen-0 samples shared across generators; see \S\ref{sec:generation}). \textbf{Binary}: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ only, eliminating the gen-0 train--test overlap. Per-gen std measures cross-generator consistency of the binary metric. The 7-feature ensemble is the strongest single-model method on both metrics and matches the best multi-detector ensemble on binary F1.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723, outperforming every individual detection baseline: +1.1\,pp over Avg-LogProb, +2.2\,pp over LD-Score, +10.7\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +19.9\,pp over Binoculars ($p < 0.001$ for all comparisons).
On the 3-class metric, the ensemble (0.789) similarly outperforms all single baselines, though the margins are inflated by the gen-0 overlap.

\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
Combining all four detection scores into a 4-detector ensemble yields binary F1\,=\,0.712---below the 7-feature ensemble (0.723).
The multi-detector advantage seen in 3-class evaluation (0.796 vs.\ 0.789) is driven entirely by superior gen-0 classification; existing detectors excel at human-vs-machine discrimination but do not capture the finer depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+.
Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble raises binary F1 to 0.724, matching the 7-feature ensemble and confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
Baseline results are stable across classifier hyperparameters: using the ensemble's settings ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$) instead of the default ($100$/$3$) changes baseline F1 by less than 0.002\,pp, confirming that performance differences reflect feature informativeness rather than classifier capacity.

\paragraph{Binoculars: a non-transferable signal.}
Binoculars achieves near-random performance on the depth task (3-class F1\,=\,0.417, binary F1\,=\,0.524), confirming that cross-model perplexity ratios---the core signal in Binoculars---do not transfer to depth discrimination.


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary synthetic text detection, providing a framework for characterizing the provenance of web-crawled text at finer granularity.
Across six generators from three model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), we documented differential depth response: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble combining both feature types achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination across six base-model generators, with per-generator std of 0.051.
Cross-model chains---where each generation step uses a different generator---yield comparable performance (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), confirming that depth signal persists under the generator heterogeneity typical of real-world contamination.
We also reported that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling, establishing that, in our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting functions as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization rather than a curative tool for data selection.

Future work should extend evaluation to instruction-tuned and RLHF models, frontier-scale generators (70B+), and multilingual settings.
All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication to facilitate reproducibility.

\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723, outperforming every individual detection baseline: +1.1\,pp over Avg-LogProb, +2.2\,pp over LD-Score, +10.7\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +19.9\,pp over Binoculars ($p < 0.001$ for all comparisons).

Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble raises binary F1 to 0.724, matching the 7-feature ensemble and confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.

\paragraph{Binoculars: a non-transferable signal.}
Binoculars achieves near-random performance on the depth task (3-class F1\,=\,0.417, binary F1\,=\,0.524), confirming that cross-model perplexity ratios---the core signal in Binoculars---do not transfer to depth discrimination.


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.789 (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), the gen-0 class F1 (0.94) may be inflated; we therefore report a leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, F1\,=\,0.723) as the primary metric in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}.
Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.

\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+0.8\,pp to 0.810), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.

\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).

\paragraph{Cross-model chains.}
Real-world contamination involves diverse generators at each depth step.
We construct cross-model chains where each generation step uses a randomly selected generator and evaluate under 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
Cross-model chains yield 3-class macro-F1\,=\,0.809 and binary F1\,=\,0.764, confirming that depth signal is maintained when chain provenance is heterogeneous.
Cross-model 3-class F1 (0.809) falls below the best single-model ceiling (Pythia-1B, 0.862) but demonstrates that depth fingerprinting remains effective in multi-generator scenarios that better approximate real-world web contamination.

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Held-out F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia & 1.0B & 0.856 & [0.843, 0.863] \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia & 2.8B & 0.804 & [0.793, 0.813] \\
OLMo-2-1B      & OLMo   & 1.5B & 0.764 & [0.754, 0.776] \\
Qwen3-0.6B     & Qwen   & 0.6B & 0.824 & [0.813, 0.834] \\
Qwen3-1.7B     & Qwen   & 1.7B & 0.806 & [0.796, 0.817] \\
Qwen3-8B       & Qwen   & 8.2B & 0.683 & [0.668, 0.694] \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (6-gen LOGO)} & 0.789 & --- \\
\multicolumn{3}{l}{5-gen LOGO (excl.\ Qwen3-8B)} & 0.802 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals ($n$\,=\,1000) for 3-class depth estimation using the 7-feature ensemble. Each row holds out one generator for testing and trains on the remaining five.}
\label{tab:logo-results}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Ordinal regression comparison.}
To test whether the ordinal structure of the 3-class depth label provides additional discriminative power, we compare CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral_ordinal} and Frank-Hall ordinal reduction \cite{frank_hall_ordinal} against the standard multiclass XGBoost classifier under the same LOGO protocol.
On 3-class F1, CORAL achieves 0.771, Frank-Hall 0.793, and XGBoost 0.789; all three confidence intervals overlap.
Binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) similarly shows no separation: XGBoost 0.721, CORAL 0.728.
Concordance index---an ordinal-specific metric rewarding correct ranking---yields XGBoost 0.821, CORAL 0.810, Frank-Hall 0.825; again, all CIs overlap.
The standard multiclass classifier already captures the depth-discriminative signal, and explicitly encoding ordinal structure does not yield a measurable gain, likely because the 3-class granularity provides insufficient ordinal resolution for ranking-aware losses to exploit.


\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Central-tendency and diversity features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show strong monotonic drift, while shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain near-stationary.}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),
while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.089$).

Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).

Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.

\centering
\small

\toprule
\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
\midrule

Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Feature ablation (6-gen LOGO). Full $>$ surface = reference confirms complementarity between surface diversity features and reference-model distributional features.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Leave-one-feature-out analysis confirms that 6 of 7 features contribute positively, with entropy\_max showing the largest marginal impact despite modest split frequency (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.png}
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals for each detection baseline and the 7-feature ensemble. Per-generator held-out F1 varies more for single detectors than for the ensemble.}
\label{fig:baseline-ci}
\end{figure}

We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation.
Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), 3-class LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
We therefore report both 3-class and binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) results; the binary metric is the primary measure of depth discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

\midrule
7-feature ensemble    & 0.789 & \textbf{0.723} & 0.051 \\

LD-Score              & 0.655 & 0.701 & 0.045 \\
FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & 0.616 & 0.056 \\
Binoculars            & 0.417 & 0.524 & 0.022 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Depth classification under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. \textbf{3-class}: gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ (gen-0 samples shared across generators; see \S\ref{sec:generation}). \textbf{Binary}: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ only, eliminating the gen-0 train--test overlap. \label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

Combining all four detection scores into a 4-detector ensemble yields binary F1\,=\,0.712---below the 7-feature ensemble (0.723).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
Sampling ablation supports this account: depth signal is robust to moderate sampling variation (F1 range ${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades at extreme temperatures ($t = 1.0$, $-6$\,pp), consistent with shape features being determined by the sampling mechanism (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}).
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
Cross-model chain evaluation (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirms that depth signal persists even when chains involve heterogeneous generators, supporting applicability to realistic web-contamination scenarios.
Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.

\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated human editing: random token replacement at 20\% reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) remains nearly unchanged ($\Delta \leq 0.8$\,pp).
LLM rephrasing presents a different challenge---3-class degradation is modest ($-3.4$\,pp), but binary F1 drops 6.3\,pp, indicating that systematic distributional manipulation erodes depth signal more effectively than surface noise (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
This asymmetry has practical implications: depth fingerprinting is robust to casual editing but more vulnerable in settings where LLM-assisted rewriting is prevalent.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.

OLMo-Instruct breaks this joint structure, and the resulting signal conflict may account for the classification collapse.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).

Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

We evaluate three prompt types (continuation, elaboration, rewriting; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}) but all share the same Pythia-2.8B generator.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.789 (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), the gen-0 class F1 (0.94) may be inflated; we therefore report a leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, F1\,=\,0.723) as the primary metric in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}.
Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.

\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+0.8\,pp to 0.810), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.

\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).

\paragraph{Cross-model chains.}
Real-world contamination involves diverse generators at each depth step.
We construct cross-model chains where each generation step uses a randomly selected generator and evaluate under 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
Cross-model chains yield 3-class macro-F1\,=\,0.809 and binary F1\,=\,0.764, confirming that depth signal is maintained when chain provenance is heterogeneous.
Cross-model 3-class F1 (0.809) falls below the best single-model ceiling (Pythia-1B, 0.862) but demonstrates that depth fingerprinting remains effective in multi-generator scenarios that better approximate real-world web contamination.

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Held-out F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia & 1.0B & 0.856 & [0.843, 0.863] \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia & 2.8B & 0.804 & [0.793, 0.813] \\
OLMo-2-1B      & OLMo   & 1.5B & 0.764 & [0.754, 0.776] \\
Qwen3-0.6B     & Qwen   & 0.6B & 0.824 & [0.813, 0.834] \\
Qwen3-1.7B     & Qwen   & 1.7B & 0.806 & [0.796, 0.817] \\
Qwen3-8B       & Qwen   & 8.2B & 0.683 & [0.668, 0.694] \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (6-gen LOGO)} & 0.789 & --- \\
\multicolumn{3}{l}{5-gen LOGO (excl.\ Qwen3-8B)} & 0.802 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals ($n$\,=\,1000) for 3-class depth estimation using the 7-feature ensemble. Each row holds out one generator for testing and trains on the remaining five.}
\label{tab:logo-results}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Ordinal regression comparison.}
To test whether the ordinal structure of the 3-class depth label provides additional discriminative power, we compare CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral_ordinal} and Frank-Hall ordinal reduction \cite{frank_hall_ordinal} against the standard multiclass XGBoost classifier under the same LOGO protocol.
On 3-class F1, CORAL achieves 0.771, Frank-Hall 0.793, and XGBoost 0.789; all three confidence intervals overlap.
Binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) similarly shows no separation: XGBoost 0.721, CORAL 0.728.
Concordance index---an ordinal-specific metric rewarding correct ranking---yields XGBoost 0.821, CORAL 0.810, Frank-Hall 0.825; again, all CIs overlap.

\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Central-tendency and diversity features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show strong monotonic drift, while shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain near-stationary.}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.269), followed by entropy mean (0.164) and TTR (0.159).
Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
\midrule
Full (7 features)     & 0.789 & hapax\_ratio (0.269) \\
Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Feature ablation (6-gen LOGO). Full $>$ surface = reference confirms complementarity between surface diversity features and reference-model distributional features.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Leave-one-feature-out analysis confirms that 6 of 7 features contribute positively, with entropy\_max showing the largest marginal impact despite modest split frequency (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.png}
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals for each detection baseline and the 7-feature ensemble. Per-generator held-out F1 varies more for single detectors than for the ensemble.}
\label{fig:baseline-ci}
\end{figure}

We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation.
Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), 3-class LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
We therefore report both 3-class and binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) results; the binary metric is the primary measure of depth discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{Per-gen std} \\
\midrule
7-feature ensemble    & 0.789 & \textbf{0.723} & 0.051 \\
4-det.\ + surface     & \textbf{0.805} & 0.724 & 0.049 \\
4-detector ens.\      & 0.796 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
Avg-LogProb           & 0.737 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
LD-Score              & 0.655 & 0.701 & 0.045 \\
FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & 0.616 & 0.056 \\
Binoculars            & 0.417 & 0.524 & 0.022 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Depth classification under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. \textbf{3-class}: gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ (gen-0 samples shared across generators; see \S\ref{sec:generation}). \textbf{Binary}: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ only, eliminating the gen-0 train--test overlap. Per-gen std measures cross-generator consistency of the binary metric. The 7-feature ensemble is the strongest single-model method on both metrics and matches the best multi-detector ensemble on binary F1.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723, outperforming every individual detection baseline: +1.1\,pp over Avg-LogProb, +2.2\,pp over LD-Score, +10.7\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +19.9\,pp over Binoculars ($p < 0.001$ for all comparisons).
On the 3-class metric, the ensemble (0.789) similarly outperforms all single baselines, though the margins are inflated by the gen-0 overlap.

\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
Combining all four detection scores into a 4-detector ensemble yields binary F1\,=\,0.712---below the 7-feature ensemble (0.723).
The multi-detector advantage seen in 3-class evaluation (0.796 vs.\ 0.789) is driven entirely by superior gen-0 classification; existing detectors excel at human-vs-machine discrimination but do not capture the finer depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+.
Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble raises binary F1 to 0.724, matching the 7-feature ensemble and confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
Baseline results are stable across classifier hyperparameters: using the ensemble's settings ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$) instead of the default ($100$/$3$) changes baseline F1 by less than 0.002\,pp, confirming that performance differences reflect feature informativeness rather than classifier capacity.

\paragraph{Binoculars: a non-transferable signal.}
Binoculars achieves near-random performance on the depth task (3-class F1\,=\,0.417, binary F1\,=\,0.524), confirming that cross-model perplexity ratios---the core signal in Binoculars---do not transfer to depth discrimination.


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
Sampling ablation supports this account: depth signal is robust to moderate sampling variation (F1 range ${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades at extreme temperatures ($t = 1.0$, $-6$\,pp), consistent with shape features being determined by the sampling mechanism (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}).
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
Cross-model chain evaluation (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirms that depth signal persists even when chains involve heterogeneous generators, supporting applicability to realistic web-contamination scenarios.
Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.

\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated human editing: random token replacement at 20\% reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) remains nearly unchanged ($\Delta \leq 0.8$\,pp).
LLM rephrasing presents a different challenge---3-class degradation is modest ($-3.4$\,pp), but binary F1 drops 6.3\,pp, indicating that systematic distributional manipulation erodes depth signal more effectively than surface noise (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
This asymmetry has practical implications: depth fingerprinting is robust to casual editing but more vulnerable in settings where LLM-assisted rewriting is prevalent.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.

\paragraph{Depth features vs.\ multi-detector ensembles.}
In 3-class evaluation, multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 (0.805 with surface features added vs.\ 0.789).
However, this advantage is driven entirely by gen-0 classification, where detection scores excel at human-vs-machine discrimination.
In the leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), the 7-feature ensemble matches the best multi-detector configuration (0.723 vs.\ 0.724), demonstrating that depth features capture the gen-1/gen-2+ distinction as effectively as four detection pipelines combined.
Depth features additionally offer interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern---and computational efficiency, requiring only a single lightweight reference model.

\paragraph{Same-family reference bias.}
Pythia-1B achieves the highest held-out F1 (0.856) despite using a same-family reference model (Pythia-410M).
Cross-family references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) yield nearly identical Pythia-1B F1 (0.845--0.848), confirming that this generator's high detectability reflects its intrinsic generation patterns rather than reference-model family bias.

\paragraph{Instruct tuning degrades depth signal through multiple mechanisms.}
Preliminary experiments with instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 for base OLMo-2-1B), and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template yields F1\,=\,0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 for the base model).
Length-controlled analysis reveals two distinct patterns.
Entropy-based features reverse sign in two of three instruct models (partial $\rho$ = +0.161, +0.364 for Qwen3-1.7B and OLMo-Instruct respectively), suggesting a genuine shift in the generation process that survives length control.
Qwen3-0.6B's depth signal becomes negligible after length control (all partial $|\rho| < 0.02$), indicating that its apparent depth response is predominantly a length artifact.
OLMo-Instruct's substantially larger residual ($+0.364$) likely reflects differences in alignment recipe rather than parameter count alone.
Surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) show model-dependent behavior: Qwen3-1.7B retains weakly positive partial correlations with depth (TTR partial $\rho$ = +0.130; hapax partial $\rho$ = +0.166), while OLMo-Instruct exhibits negative correlations similar to base models (TTR partial $\rho = -0.241$; hapax partial $\rho = -0.198$).
This divergence cautions against treating surface feature reversal as a universal consequence of instruction tuning; the effect is architecture- or training-recipe-dependent.

OLMo-Instruct presents a paradox: it exhibits the strongest entropy--depth partial correlation (+0.364) yet the worst classification performance (LOGO F1\,=\,0.338).
A likely explanation is that its surface features retain base-model polarity (negative partial $\rho$) while entropy reverses to positive, creating contradictory signals for a classifier trained on base-model patterns---where entropy and surface features are jointly negative at greater depths.
OLMo-Instruct breaks this joint structure, and the resulting signal conflict may account for the classification collapse.
Disentangling these mechanisms across a broader set of instruct models is a priority for future work; the current findings justify restricting our scope to base models where such confounds are minimal.
